bhūtamātā
(‘Mother of beings’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as the मोथेर् is an ancient practice in हिन्दुइस्म्. One of her innumerable aspects is ‘Bhūtamātā’ or the ‘Mother of Beings’. Though she is consi-dered as the मोथेर् of all the living beings she is most probably the deity of less known or obscure cults supposed to be worshipped by bhūtas (goblins), pretas and piśācas (disembodied spirits) and minor godlings.
Iconographically she is shown as sitting under an अश्वत्थ tree (Ficus religiosa) on a splendid throne wearing ornaments of pearls. She has two arms carrying a sword and a shield. Her complexion is pinkish white.

bhūtaśuddhi
(‘purification of the elements’)
------------------------------------------
Pūjā or worship of a deity, whether in a temple or at home, is an elaborate ritual. This पूजा can be based either on the Vedic traditions or on the tāntric.
One of the preliminary processes in a tāntric पूजा is ‘bhūtaśuddhi’ or purification of the elements, making up the body of the worshipper.
The worshipper has to raise his own self, the jīvātman, first to the feet of the Lord (Paramaśiva or परमात्मन्) dwelling in the सहस्रार or thousand petalled lotus in the head. Then, uttering the मन्त्र yaṁ, has to imagine that the dross in his body has dried up. This should be followed by the burning up this dross through the मन्त्र raṁ. The drossless body is then to be bathed in ambrosia, uttering the मन्त्र vaṁ and completely regenerated by the मन्त्र laṁ. This purified and regenerated body is now fit to worship the Lord.
This whole process is called ‘bhūtaśuddhi.’

bhūtayajña
(‘sacrifice unto the animals’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu scriptures emphasize that man is essentially a social being. He is born in this world with ऋणत्रय or three debts on his head, to discharge which, he has to perform पञ्चयज्ञस् or the five daily sacrifices. These पञ्चयज्ञस् are a compulsory part of a householder’s life.
The last of these five daily sacrifices is भूतयज्ञ. Bhūtas are living beings, especially the animals. Feeding the animals, both the domestic and the stray, according to one’s capacity comprises this यज्ञ. Since the Lord is the indwelling spirit of all the living beings, feeding the hungry souls—whether the human beings or the animals—will please him. This is one of the best ways to discharge one’s debts. It will also contribute to the awareness that ultimately the whole universe is one and that we are part of that oneness.
See also PAÑCAYAJÑAS and ṚṆATRAYA.

bhūtagaṇa
(‘troupe of goblins’)
------------------------------------------
Bhūtas are grotesque goblins who form part of the army of रुद्र-शिव. Nīlalohita रुद्र (one of the aspects of शिव) is said to have created eleven crores of bhūtas. They are generally pictured as lean figures with elongated ears eager to trouble others. They often fought the असुरस् or demons siding with the gods.
Being the lord of these bhūtas, शिव is often called ‘Bhūtanātha,’ ‘Bhūteśa’ or ‘Bhūteśvara’. गणपति and Nandikeśvara also are sometimes called by this name.

bhūta
(‘that which is produced,’ ‘that which has become’)
------------------------------------------
One of the more widely used terms in the Indian philosophical systems, the word ‘bhūta’ refers to the five fundamental ele-ments—pañcabhūtas—viz., पृथ्वी (earth), ap (water), तेजस् (fire), वायु (air) and आकाश (ether), the permutations and combi-nations of which result in this physical universe.
These bhūtas have two aspects, the primary and the secondary. In the primary aspect they are ‘sūkṣmabhūtas’ or ‘tan-mātras’. They arise from the आत्मन् associated with अज्ञान or nescience and are called so since each one of them contains only that quality. For instance, the primordial element आकाश has only शब्द (sound or vibration) as its characteristic and hence is called the ‘śabda-tanmātra’. The other primordial elements are: sparśa-tanmātra (vāyu or air), rūpa-tanmātra (agni or fire), रस-tanmātra (ap or water) and गन्ध-तन्मात्र (pṛthvī or earth).
When these five primordial elements combine among themselves by the process of पञ्चीकरण or quintuplication (See PAÑCĪKARAṆA for details.) they produce the secondary elements, the gross ones, more commonly called the ‘mahābhūtas or sthūlabhūtas’. Further च्रेअतिओन् takes place out of them, associated of course, with the आत्मन्.
The word भूत is also applied to all the living beings as a general term.
Another meaning of the word is ‘spirits, ghosts and goblins,’ belief in whose existence was widespread. They are generally malignant, live upon flesh, roam about mostly during the nights and haunt forests, desolate houses and बुरिअल् or च्रेमतिओन् grounds.
Persons who meet with violent death or commit सुइचिदे or for whom no obsequial rites are performed after death, are supposed to become bhūtas or pretas or piśācas (disembodied spirits). Performing such rites or prayers to God by the living, will help them to be liberated from that miserable state.
The art and science of controlling these spirits and using them for fulfilling one’s desires or harming others, called ‘bhūtavidyā’ has been in existence since Vedic times.
One of the eight sections of आयुर्वेद, the science of health and longevity, is also designated as ‘Bhūtavidyā.’ It deals with the treatment of psychological ailments, believed to be caused by malevolent spirits.

Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra
------------------------------------------
This is a small work belonging to the वामाचार tantra group.
‘Bhūta’ means any ‘living being’. ‘Ḍāmara’ means ‘terrible.’ Hence Bhūta-डामर Tantra means a work that can strike terror in the hearts of those beings against whom it may be used.
It has sixteen paṭalas or chapters and 284 verses. This number, however, is deceptive, since several verses have 10 to 20 lines!
The contents may be briefly stated as follows:
Process of killing and reviving a person (māraṇa and sañjīvana); method of pleasing the goddess who lives in च्रेमतिओन् grounds (smaśānavāsinī); mantras of deities like Caṇḍakātyāyanī and Krodhapati; mantras and rites that help the sādhaka to bring certain spirit-deities like Ceṭikā and Bhūtinī under control; mantras by which even gods like इन्द्र, विष्णु and महेश्वर can be eliminated; mantras of eight Yakṣiṇīs like Surasundarī, Kanaka-vatī and others who, when pleased, will fulfil all the desires of the sādhakas.

bhūtajaya
(‘conquest of the elements’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B.C.) is an accredited work on the philosophy and practise of योग. The third chapter of this work designated as Vibhūti-pāda (the section dealing with supernatural powers) gives an account of many yogic powers and the means of attaining them. One such power mentioned there (3.44 and 45) is ‘bhūtajaya.’
Bhūtas are the five elements: पृथ्वी or earth, ap or water, तेजस् or fire, वायु or air and आकाश or ether. When a योगि practises सṁयम on them, he conquers them.
Saṁyama is the technical name given to the trio of धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (superconscious revelation).
If सṁयम is achieved on the भूत पृथ्वी or earth, he conquers it. As a result, the solidity of the earth will not be an obstacle to his free movement. Similarly the conquest of the भूत water gives him immunity against wetness, of fire, immunity against burning and so on.

bhūtavidyā
(‘demonology’)
------------------------------------------
Works on आयुर्वेद (science of health and longevity) generally deal with eight subjects, one of which is ‘bhūtavidyā.’ It is the ancient equivalent of the modern psychiatry. Mental disorders, it was believed, were caused by bhūtas or malevolent spirits. The remedies recommended were prayers, oblations, exorcism as also some drugs.
See also ĀYURVEDA.
Bhūtavidyā is one of the nineteen branches of Knowledge (vidyās) mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (

bhūtarutajñāna
(‘knowledge of the sounds of animals’)
------------------------------------------
Man alone, among all the living beings, has had the privilege of being endowed with the power of speech, with which he can convey his thoughts and feelings to others. However he has even been curious to know whether animals, birds and even worms have their own means of communication. पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) the ancient teacher of योग, asserts in his famous work, the Yogasūtras (3.17), that a योगि can acquire that extraordinary power by practising सṁयम (See BHŪTAJAYA for an explanation of this word.) on the three separate aspects of every word.
This can be illustrated with an example. When a person utters the word ‘cow’ we get the knowledge of a cow. However, on analysis, we find that three things are involved in this. The word itself is a sound produced by uttering the three letters c, o and w, in succession by the vocal organs. The animal cow is a solid external object perceptible to the eyes and the hands. The knowledge of it produced in the मिन्द् is of the form of mental waves. Ordinarily, these three are mixed up and yet, give us a unitive experience.
If the योगि can manage to separate these three in his मिन्द् and practise सṁयम on each of them separately, then, he realizes the basic truths underlying each of them, viz., शब्द (sound), अर्थ (object signified) and pratyaya (knowledge in the form of mental waves). This will now empower him to ‘know’ the meaning of all the sounds uttered by all the living beings including those of the animal kingdom.
Purāṇas sometimes mention the names of persons who had acquired this power.
